question: A tenant signs a lease for a retail space with a definite start date and a definite end date exactly 36 months later. What type of leasehold estate has been created?
choice_a: Estate for years
choice_b: Periodic tenancy
choice_c: Tenancy at will
choice_d: Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: An estate (tenancy) for years is any leasehold with a fixed, agreed-upon beginning and ending date. Despite the name, it can last for any specific length of time, even less than a year, as long as the term is certain.
source_note: Standard national real estate pre-licensing content on leasehold estates; general common-law property doctrine (see e.g. Wikipedia 'Leasehold estate' summary of estate for years), not Oregon-specific statute.

question: Because an estate for years has a definite termination date fixed in the lease, which of the following is generally true about ending the tenancy?
choice_a: The tenancy ends automatically on the stated date, and no notice to terminate is legally required
choice_b: Either party must give at least 30 days' written notice before the end date
choice_c: The lease automatically renews for an identical term unless the landlord objects
choice_d: A court order is always required to end the tenancy
explanation: Because the term and ending date are already certain from the start, an estate for years terminates automatically at the expiration of that stated term without either party needing to give notice.
source_note: General real estate principles textbook content on estate-for-years termination; common-law rule, not tied to Oregon statute.

question: A tenant rents an apartment on a month-to-month basis, paying rent on the first of each month with no stated ending date. What kind of leasehold estate is this?
choice_a: Periodic tenancy
choice_b: Estate for years
choice_c: Tenancy at sufferance
choice_d: Freehold estate
explanation: A periodic tenancy (such as month-to-month or year-to-year) automatically renews for successive, equal periods until one party gives proper notice to terminate. It is defined by the interval at which rent is paid rather than a fixed overall term.
source_note: General real estate leasehold estate content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Leasehold estate' description of periodic tenancy as defined by the rent-payment interval.

question: Under the common-law default rule, how much advance notice is generally required to terminate a periodic tenancy?
choice_a: Notice equal in length to the period of tenancy (e.g., 30 days for a month-to-month tenancy)
choice_b: No notice is ever required
choice_c: A fixed 90 days regardless of the rental period
choice_d: Notice may only be given verbally and takes effect immediately
explanation: The general common-law rule is that notice to terminate a periodic tenancy must equal the length of the periodic term itself, so a month-to-month tenancy typically requires about a month's notice. Specific statutory notice periods vary by state and can differ from this default.
source_note: General common-law property principle taught in national pre-licensing curricula; a default rule, not a specific Oregon statutory notice period.

question: A property owner allows a family member to live in a vacant house rent-free with no lease and no set term, and either party may end the arrangement at any time upon reasonable notice. This describes which leasehold estate?
choice_a: Tenancy at will
choice_b: Estate for years
choice_c: Periodic tenancy
choice_d: Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: A tenancy at will has no fixed term and no set rent-payment interval, and it continues only as long as both parties agree; either the landlord or the tenant may end it by giving reasonable notice.
source_note: General real estate leasehold estate content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Leasehold estate' description of tenancy at will.

question: Which of the following events will generally terminate a tenancy at will by operation of law?
choice_a: The death of either the landlord or the tenant
choice_b: The tenant paying rent one day late
choice_c: The landlord repainting the exterior of the building
choice_d: The tenant adding a houseplant to the premises
explanation: Because a tenancy at will depends on the continuing personal agreement of both parties, it ends automatically upon the death of either party, an attempted assignment, waste committed by the tenant, or a transfer of the landlord's interest in the property.
source_note: General common-law property doctrine on tenancy at will termination; standard national pre-licensing content.

question: A tenant's one-year lease expires, but the tenant remains in possession and continues paying rent without the landlord's consent to a new agreement. What leasehold estate does this create?
choice_a: Tenancy at sufferance
choice_b: Estate for years
choice_c: Tenancy at will
choice_d: Fee simple estate
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant who lawfully took possession wrongfully 'holds over' in the property after the lease term ends, without the landlord's permission. It is the lowest form of leasehold interest.
source_note: General real estate leasehold estate content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Leasehold estate' description of tenancy at sufferance (holdover tenant).

question: How does a holdover tenant (tenancy at sufferance) differ from a trespasser?
choice_a: The holdover tenant originally took possession lawfully under a valid lease, while a trespasser never had the landlord's permission to occupy the property
choice_b: A trespasser pays rent while a holdover tenant does not
choice_c: There is no legal distinction between the two
choice_d: A holdover tenant automatically owns the property after one year
explanation: The key distinction is how possession began: a holdover tenant entered lawfully under a lease and simply stayed past its expiration, whereas a trespasser never had any right to occupy the property in the first place.
source_note: General common-law property doctrine distinguishing tenancy at sufferance from trespass; standard national pre-licensing content.

question: When a lease ends and a tenant does not vacate, which of the following options does a landlord generally have?
choice_a: Evict the holdover tenant or accept rent and treat the arrangement as a new periodic tenancy
choice_b: The landlord has no legal recourse and must wait indefinitely
choice_c: The landlord automatically forfeits ownership of the property
choice_d: The original lease terms become permanently void with no landlord remedy
explanation: A landlord facing a holdover tenant typically may pursue eviction through legal process, or may choose to accept the tenant's continued rent payments, which generally converts the arrangement into a new periodic tenancy (sometimes at an increased rent).
source_note: General property management/leasehold principle; consistent with Wikipedia 'Leasehold estate' discussion of holdover tenancy outcomes.

question: The landlord's covenant of quiet enjoyment, implied in essentially every lease, primarily protects the tenant's right to:
choice_a: Possess and use the leased premises without substantial interference from the landlord or someone with a superior title
choice_b: Pay a reduced rent after the first year of occupancy
choice_c: Sublet the unit to anyone without landlord consent
choice_d: Receive free utilities for the length of the lease
explanation: The covenant of quiet enjoyment is an implied promise that the tenant will be able to possess and use the property without substantial interference from the landlord, someone claiming a superior title, or (in most cases) actions the landlord fails to remedy.
source_note: General landlord-tenant common-law doctrine, standard national real estate pre-licensing content; not an Oregon-specific statutory provision.

question: A landlord's conditions render a rented unit so unsafe or unlivable that the tenant is forced to move out, even though the landlord never formally files to remove the tenant. This situation best describes:
choice_a: Constructive eviction
choice_b: Actual eviction
choice_c: Tenancy at sufferance
choice_d: A percentage lease default
explanation: Constructive eviction occurs when a landlord's act or serious neglect (such as failing to maintain habitable conditions) so substantially interferes with the tenant's use and enjoyment of the property that the tenant is justified in vacating, even absent a formal eviction filing.
source_note: General landlord-tenant common-law doctrine on constructive eviction; standard national pre-licensing content, not Oregon-specific.

question: Actual eviction, as distinguished from constructive eviction, refers to:
choice_a: A landlord's formal legal action to physically remove a tenant and regain possession of the premises
choice_b: A tenant voluntarily choosing to move out early
choice_c: A tenant subletting the unit to a third party
choice_d: A landlord raising the rent at lease renewal
explanation: Actual eviction is the formal legal process by which a landlord obtains a court judgment and, ultimately, an order directing law enforcement to physically remove a tenant from the premises, as opposed to constructive eviction, which involves no such formal removal.
source_note: General landlord-tenant/eviction terminology; standard national pre-licensing content.

question: The implied warranty of habitability generally obligates a residential landlord to:
choice_a: Maintain the rental premises in a condition fit for basic human habitation, such as functioning plumbing, heat, and structural safety
choice_b: Provide the tenant with new furniture every lease term
choice_c: Guarantee the tenant a specific resale value for any improvements made
choice_d: Personally reside on the property during the lease term
explanation: Most residential leases carry an implied warranty of habitability, meaning the landlord must keep the property in a condition that meets basic standards of safety and livability, regardless of whether the lease expressly says so.
source_note: General landlord-tenant common-law/statutory doctrine widely recognized across states; standard national pre-licensing content, not tied to Oregon's specific landlord-tenant code.

question: Among a tenant's basic obligations under a typical lease, which duty most directly protects the landlord's reversionary interest in the property?
choice_a: The duty to avoid committing waste that would damage or diminish the value of the premises
choice_b: The duty to attend all homeowners' association meetings
choice_c: The duty to purchase the landlord's liability insurance policy
choice_d: The duty to pay property taxes directly to the county assessor
explanation: A tenant generally has a duty not to commit waste, meaning they must not damage the property or allow it to deteriorate beyond normal wear and tear, since the landlord retains a reversionary interest expecting the property back in reasonable condition.
source_note: General landlord-tenant common-law doctrine on waste and tenant duties; standard national pre-licensing content.

question: When a leasehold estate ends, the ownership interest that returns to the landlord (the original fee owner) is known as a:
choice_a: Reversion
choice_b: Remainder
choice_c: Easement
choice_d: License
explanation: A reversion is the future interest retained by the landlord (grantor) that automatically returns full possessory rights to the landlord when the leasehold estate terminates.
source_note: General real property estates/future interests concept from national pre-licensing curricula.

question: In a gross lease, which party is generally responsible for paying the property's operating expenses, such as taxes, insurance, and maintenance?
choice_a: The landlord, out of the fixed rent the tenant pays
choice_b: The tenant, in addition to the base rent
choice_c: The property management company, out of its own commission
choice_d: The local government, through a special assessment
explanation: In a gross lease, the tenant pays one flat, fixed rent amount, and the landlord is responsible for covering the building's operating expenses such as property taxes, insurance, and maintenance out of that rent.
source_note: General commercial/residential lease structure content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Net lease' description of gross lease as the counterpart to net leases.

question: A net lease differs from a gross lease chiefly in that:
choice_a: The tenant pays some or all of the property's operating expenses in addition to base rent
choice_b: The landlord pays the tenant a stipend for occupying the space
choice_c: Rent is calculated solely as a percentage of the tenant's gross sales
choice_d: The lease automatically terminates if property taxes increase
explanation: Under a net lease, the tenant pays base rent plus some or all of the expenses that would otherwise fall on the property owner (such as taxes, insurance, and/or maintenance), which is why the landlord's rental income is described as 'net' of those pass-through costs.
source_note: General commercial lease structure content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Net lease' summary of gross vs. net lease distinction.

question: Under a single net lease (often called an 'N' lease), the tenant typically pays base rent plus which additional expense?
choice_a: Property taxes only
choice_b: Property taxes, building insurance, and maintenance
choice_c: A percentage of the tenant's gross sales
choice_d: The landlord's mortgage principal payments
explanation: A single net (N) lease requires the tenant to pay property taxes in addition to base rent, while the landlord remains responsible for insurance, maintenance, and structural repairs. This lease type is relatively uncommon compared to double or triple net leases.
source_note: General commercial lease structure content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Net lease' description of single net (N) leases.

question: In a double net lease (an 'NN' lease), the tenant is generally responsible for paying base rent plus which two additional costs?
choice_a: Property taxes and building insurance
choice_b: Maintenance and the landlord's income tax
choice_c: A percentage of gross sales and common area maintenance only
choice_d: Structural repairs and the landlord's mortgage interest
explanation: Under a double net (NN) lease, the tenant pays base rent plus property taxes and building insurance premiums, while the landlord typically remains responsible for structural repairs and common area maintenance.
source_note: General commercial lease structure content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Net lease' description of double net (NN) leases.

question: A triple net (NNN) lease, common for freestanding commercial and retail buildings, shifts responsibility for which expenses to the tenant?
choice_a: Property taxes, building insurance, and maintenance/common area costs
choice_b: Only the landlord's property management fee
choice_c: Only the cost of the tenant's own trade fixtures
choice_d: The landlord's capital gains tax upon eventual sale of the building
explanation: In a triple net (NNN) lease, the tenant pays base rent plus all three major property expense categories: real estate taxes, building insurance, and maintenance (including common area maintenance). This structure is widely used for freestanding retail and commercial buildings.
source_note: General commercial lease structure content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Net lease' description of triple net (NNN) leases as the most common form for freestanding commercial buildings.

question: A percentage lease, typically used for retail space in shopping centers, bases all or part of the rent on:
choice_a: A percentage of the tenant's gross sales generated at the leased premises
choice_b: A percentage of the landlord's total property portfolio value
choice_c: A fixed percentage increase tied only to the Consumer Price Index
choice_d: A percentage of the tenant's net personal income
explanation: A percentage lease ties some or all of the rent to a percentage of the tenant's gross sales made on the premises, often structured as a base minimum rent plus a percentage of sales above a specified breakpoint. It is common in retail and shopping center leasing.
source_note: General commercial retail lease structure content, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum topic.

question: In a typical percentage lease with a stated 'breakpoint,' the tenant generally pays:
choice_a: A minimum base rent plus a percentage of gross sales that exceed the breakpoint amount
choice_b: Only a percentage of sales with no minimum guaranteed rent to the landlord
choice_c: A flat rent that never varies regardless of sales performance
choice_d: Rent calculated as a percentage of the landlord's operating costs
explanation: Percentage leases commonly include a natural or negotiated 'breakpoint' — the sales level at which percentage rent begins. The tenant pays a guaranteed minimum base rent, plus a percentage of gross sales above that breakpoint.
source_note: General commercial retail lease structure content, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum topic on percentage-lease breakpoints.

question: A rent escalation clause in a commercial lease is designed to:
choice_a: Increase the tenant's rent over time according to a pre-set schedule or index, such as the Consumer Price Index
choice_b: Permanently freeze rent at the initial lease rate
choice_c: Automatically terminate the lease if the tenant's business grows
choice_d: Require the landlord to pay the tenant a rebate each year
explanation: An escalation clause allows rent to increase during the lease term based on a predetermined schedule (fixed step-ups) or an external index such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), helping the landlord's rental income keep pace with rising costs.
source_note: General commercial lease terminology, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum topic on lease escalation clauses.

question: A Principal Broker hired by an owner to manage a residential rental property is acting in what legal capacity toward the owner?
choice_a: As a fiduciary agent, owing duties of loyalty, care, obedience, accounting, and disclosure
choice_b: As an independent third party with no special duties to either the owner or tenants
choice_c: As a co-owner of the property with equal decision-making authority
choice_d: As a guarantor personally liable for all of the owner's mortgage payments
explanation: A property manager acting under a management agreement is an agent of the owner and owes the owner fiduciary duties, commonly summarized as loyalty, obedience (to lawful instructions), disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care and skill.
source_note: General agency/property management fiduciary duty content, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum; consistent with Wikipedia 'Property manager' description of the manager's primary responsibility to the owner. 'Principal Broker' terminology used per Oregon's license-tier convention for this track.

question: As part of the fiduciary duty of accounting, a property manager handling an owner's rental income should:
choice_a: Keep accurate records of all funds received and disbursed and provide the owner periodic financial reports
choice_b: Deposit all rents collected directly into the manager's personal checking account for convenience
choice_c: Avoid disclosing any financial details to the owner unless subpoenaed
choice_d: Combine owner funds from multiple properties into one undocumented cash reserve
explanation: The fiduciary duty of accounting requires a property manager to maintain accurate, transparent records of rents collected and expenses paid, and to make periodic reports to the owner, consistent with the manager's role as the owner's agent.
source_note: General fiduciary duty (accounting) content in property management, standard national pre-licensing curriculum; consistent with Wikipedia 'Property manager' reference to collecting rents, paying expenses, and periodic reporting to the owner.

question: A property manager's duty of obedience to the owner generally means the manager must:
choice_a: Follow the owner's lawful instructions regarding the management of the property
choice_b: Follow every instruction from the owner even if it would violate fair housing law
choice_c: Ignore the owner's wishes whenever the manager believes a better business decision exists
choice_d: Delegate all management decisions to the tenants
explanation: The fiduciary duty of obedience requires the manager to carry out the owner's lawful instructions. It does not extend to illegal instructions — for example, a manager may not follow an owner's directive that would violate fair housing or other laws.
source_note: General fiduciary duty (obedience) content in agency/property management, standard national pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A written property management agreement between an owner and a management firm typically defines all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_a: The tenant's personal credit score requirements for an unrelated property owned by someone else
choice_b: The scope of the manager's authority (e.g., leasing, collecting rent, hiring vendors)
choice_c: The manager's compensation, such as a percentage of collected rents
choice_d: The duration of the management agreement and how it may be terminated
explanation: A management agreement is specific to the property (and owner) it covers — it defines the manager's scope of authority, compensation, and term for that engagement. It would have no bearing on tenant qualification standards for a wholly unrelated property owned by a different party.
source_note: General property management agreement content, standard national pre-licensing curriculum on management contract elements.

question: One of a property manager's core physical-asset responsibilities is to:
choice_a: Maintain and preserve the condition of the property, including arranging necessary repairs and preventive maintenance
choice_b: Decide unilaterally to sell the property without owner authorization
choice_c: Set the assessed value of the property for county tax purposes
choice_d: Personally guarantee the building against all casualty losses
explanation: Beyond financial and tenant-relations duties, a property manager is generally responsible for maintaining the physical condition of the property — arranging repairs, coordinating vendors, and preventing deterioration — to protect and preserve the owner's asset value.
source_note: General property management duties content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Property manager' description of arranging maintenance and vendor services.

question: As a general concept applicable across most jurisdictions, a security deposit collected from a tenant is primarily intended to:
choice_a: Protect the landlord against unpaid rent and damage to the unit beyond normal wear and tear
choice_b: Serve as an additional, non-refundable fee for the privilege of renting
choice_c: Automatically apply as the final month's rent unless the tenant objects
choice_d: Compensate the landlord for the tenant's use of common-area amenities only
explanation: A security deposit generally functions as financial protection for the landlord against unpaid rent or damage to the unit exceeding ordinary wear and tear; specific rules about amount limits, allowed deductions, and refund timing vary considerably by state.
source_note: General landlord-tenant/security deposit concept widely taught in national pre-licensing curricula; deliberately kept general, not tied to Oregon's specific statutory deposit rules.

question: As a general best practice and common statutory requirement, funds collected as tenant security deposits should be:
choice_a: Held separately in a trust or escrow account rather than commingled with the property manager's or broker's own operating funds
choice_b: Deposited directly into the property manager's personal savings account for safekeeping
choice_c: Spent immediately on the manager's business operating expenses
choice_d: Converted to a non-refundable administrative fee upon receipt
explanation: A widely applied general principle in property management and real estate brokerage is that client and tenant trust funds, including security deposits, must be kept in a dedicated trust or escrow account, separate from the broker's or manager's own operating funds, to avoid commingling.
source_note: General trust fund handling / anti-commingling principle common across real estate brokerage and property management regulation nationally; general concept, not citing Oregon's specific trust account statute.

question: Ordinary wear and tear on a rental unit, such as minor carpet fading from normal foot traffic, is generally treated as:
choice_a: A normal cost of ownership that a landlord typically may NOT deduct from a tenant's security deposit
choice_b: Damage the tenant must always pay to fully replace regardless of cause
choice_c: A basis for immediate eviction
choice_d: Something a tenant must insure against separately from the security deposit
explanation: Reasonable, ordinary wear and tear resulting from normal use of the property over time is generally distinguished from tenant-caused damage; landlords typically cannot deduct for ordinary wear and tear from a security deposit, only for damage beyond that standard.
source_note: General security deposit concept regarding ordinary wear and tear, standard national pre-licensing curriculum topic.

question: Before filing a formal court eviction action against a tenant, a landlord generally must first:
choice_a: Serve the tenant with a written notice to quit or cure, giving the tenant an opportunity to remedy the issue or vacate
choice_b: Change the locks while the tenant is away
choice_c: Shut off the utilities to encourage the tenant to leave
choice_d: Physically remove the tenant's belongings from the unit
explanation: The standard first step in an eviction process is for the landlord to serve the tenant with a written notice (often called a notice to quit, notice to cure, or notice to vacate) specifying the issue and the tenant's opportunity to fix it or leave before further legal action follows.
source_note: General eviction process content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Eviction' description of the required notice-to-quit phase preceding legal action.

question: If a tenant does not leave after being properly served notice, the landlord's next legal step is generally to:
choice_a: File a formal court action, often called an unlawful detainer or summary possession proceeding, to obtain a judgment for possession
choice_b: Immediately and personally remove the tenant's possessions from the unit
choice_c: Re-rent the unit to a new tenant while the current tenant is still living there
choice_d: Report the tenant to a credit bureau instead of pursuing any court process
explanation: When a tenant fails to comply with a notice to quit or cure, the landlord's recourse is to file a court case, commonly called an unlawful detainer or summary possession action, seeking a judgment awarding legal possession of the property.
source_note: General eviction process content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Eviction' description of filing a lawsuit as the step following an unheeded notice.

question: 'Self-help' eviction, such as a landlord changing the locks or shutting off utilities to force a tenant out without a court order, is:
choice_a: Generally illegal; most jurisdictions require the landlord to obtain a court judgment before removing a tenant
choice_b: A legally preferred alternative to going to court because it saves time
choice_c: Permitted anytime rent is even one day late
choice_d: Only illegal if the tenant is a senior citizen
explanation: Self-help eviction tactics — such as changing locks, removing a tenant's belongings, or shutting off utilities without a court order — are prohibited in the vast majority of jurisdictions. Landlords are generally required to use the formal legal eviction process.
source_note: General eviction process content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Eviction' statement that most jurisdictions prohibit self-help eviction without prior legal action.

question: After a landlord wins an eviction lawsuit and the tenant still refuses to leave, what document authorizes law enforcement to physically remove the tenant?
choice_a: A writ of possession (or warrant of removal)
choice_b: A quitclaim deed
choice_c: A certificate of occupancy
choice_d: A memorandum of lease
explanation: Once a landlord obtains a favorable court judgment, the final enforcement step is typically a writ of possession (sometimes called a warrant of removal), which directs law enforcement officers to carry out the physical removal of the tenant and, in many cases, their belongings.
source_note: General eviction process content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Eviction' description of the writ of possession/warrant of removal as the final enforcement step.

question: Which of the following is typically NOT, by itself, a recognized legal ground for eviction?
choice_a: The landlord simply preferring a different tenant for aesthetic reasons
choice_b: Nonpayment of rent
choice_c: A material violation of the lease terms
choice_d: Proper non-renewal of a lease at the end of its term (where permitted)
explanation: Common recognized grounds for eviction include nonpayment of rent, material lease violations, and lawful non-renewal at lease expiration. A landlord's mere personal preference for a different tenant, without a recognized legal basis, is not by itself a valid ground for eviction.
source_note: General eviction process content; consistent with Wikipedia 'Eviction' summary of common grounds such as nonpayment and lease violations.

question: When a tenant transfers their entire remaining leasehold interest to a new party for the rest of the lease term and steps out of the landlord relationship entirely, this is called a lease:
choice_a: Assignment
choice_b: Sublease
choice_c: Novation of the security deposit
choice_d: Percentage adjustment
explanation: An assignment occurs when the original tenant transfers the entire remaining term and interest in the lease to a new tenant (the assignee), who then deals directly with the landlord. The original tenant may still remain secondarily liable unless released by the landlord.
source_note: General leasehold transfer concept (assignment vs. sublease), standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: How does a sublease differ from an assignment of a lease?
choice_a: In a sublease, the original tenant transfers only part of the remaining term or premises and remains directly liable to the landlord, whereas an assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest
choice_b: A sublease always requires the landlord to release the original tenant from all liability
choice_c: There is no legal difference between the two arrangements
choice_d: An assignment can only be used for commercial leases, and a sublease only for residential leases
explanation: In a sublease, the original tenant transfers less than the full remaining interest (e.g., part of the space or a shorter time period) and remains in privity of contract with the landlord, retaining ultimate responsibility for lease obligations. An assignment, by contrast, transfers the tenant's entire remaining leasehold interest.
source_note: General leasehold transfer concept (assignment vs. sublease), standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum.

question: A 'surrender' of a lease refers to:
choice_a: A mutual agreement between landlord and tenant to terminate the lease early, before its stated expiration
choice_b: A landlord unilaterally seizing the property from a paying tenant
choice_c: The tenant's automatic loss of the security deposit at lease signing
choice_d: A court-ordered eviction for cause
explanation: Surrender is the voluntary, mutual agreement of both landlord and tenant to end a lease before its natural expiration date, releasing both parties from further obligations under the original lease term.
source_note: General lease termination concept, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum on lease surrender.

question: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for use in their business (such as display shelving or a walk-in cooler) are generally treated as:
choice_a: Personal property that the tenant may remove before the lease ends, provided the tenant repairs any resulting damage
choice_b: Real property that automatically transfers to the landlord the moment they are installed
choice_c: Items the tenant must leave behind at the landlord's request with no compensation, regardless of lease terms
choice_d: Items that void the lease if installed without a permit
explanation: Trade fixtures are items a commercial tenant installs to conduct their business. Unlike ordinary fixtures, which typically become part of the real property, trade fixtures generally remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed before or at the end of the lease term, so long as the tenant repairs any damage caused by removal.
source_note: General trade fixture doctrine, standard national real estate pre-licensing curriculum topic distinguishing trade fixtures from ordinary fixtures.

question: A Principal Broker managing several rental units for different owners has a duty of confidentiality that generally requires the broker to:
choice_a: Avoid disclosing one owner's private financial or business information to another owner or to unrelated third parties without authorization
choice_b: Share every owner's financial details freely with all current tenants
choice_c: Publish each owner's rental income figures for marketing purposes
choice_d: Disclose confidential owner information to a competing property management firm upon request
explanation: As a fiduciary, a property manager owes each principal a duty of confidentiality, meaning private financial or business information about one owner's property should not be disclosed to other owners, tenants, or third parties without proper authorization.
source_note: General fiduciary duty (confidentiality) content in agency/property management, standard national pre-licensing curriculum. 'Principal Broker' terminology used per Oregon's license-tier convention for this track.
